units.title: Cleaning and Exploring Data
units.description: Learn the essential skills of data wrangling and exploratory data analysis. You will move from handling missing values to identifying deep patterns and correlations within datasets.

lectures.title: Data Cleaning
lectures.description: This lecture addresses the messy reality of raw data, teaching you how to identify and fix common structural and content issues to ensure your analysis is based on high-quality information.

sessions.title: Missing Values
sessions.description: This session explores why data might be missing and the various strategies for handling it, such as dropping rows versus imputation. You will be able to diagnose patterns of missingness (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and choose a treatment strategy that preserves the integrity of your findings. Mastering this is critical because ignoring missing data often leads to biased conclusions in real-world projects.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by challenging the intuitive but dangerous assumption that 'no data is better than bad data.' On the whiteboard, draw a simple scatter plot with a clear trend line, then erase several random dots. Ask the students: if we just ignore these holes, do we still get the same story? This sets the stage for the concept of 'Missingness,' not as a technical nuisance, but as a potential source of catastrophic bias. Explain that in data science, 'null' is a signal in itself. If we ignore why data is missing, we are likely creating a 'Loud Silence' that skews our business decisions or scientific findings.

Introduce the three formal categories of missingness using a relatable health clinic example. Draw a table for 'Missing Completely at Random' (MCAR)—where a survey form simply fell under the desk; 'Missing at Random' (MAR)—where men might be less likely to report their weight, but we can predict that missingness using their gender; and 'Missing Not at Random' (MNAR)—where people with the highest debt are the ones refusing to answer the 'income' question. Emphasize that MNAR is the most dangerous because the reason for the missingness is tied to the value itself. Illustrate this on the board by showing how dropping the 'high debt' rows would lead a bank to believe their average customer is much wealthier than they actually are, creating a selection bias.

Transition to the 'Treatments' phase by drawing a fork in the road. On one side is 'Deletion.' Explain that while dropping rows is the easiest path, it is a luxury we can only afford if the data is MCAR. Warn against the common pitfall of 'Listwise Deletion,' where a dataset with 5% missing in 10 different columns might result in losing 50% of the total records. On the other side of the fork, introduce 'Imputation.' Visualize mean/median imputation as a 'flattening' force: if you replace all missing values with the average, you artificially shrink the variance and make your data look more certain than it really is. Use a histogram to show how imputation creates a 'spike' at the mean, which can lead to overconfident models and 'false positives' in statistical significance.

Conduct an interactive practice moment where students calculate the percentage of missingness in a conceptual dataset. Then, have them verbalize the shift in the 'Mean' after a dummy imputation. The goal here is to reveal the 'Price of Convenience': by filling in a gap, we have technically 'lied' to the model to keep the machinery running. Conclude by framing the choice of strategy as a trade-off between power (keeping more data) and purity (avoiding bias). The most important takeaway should be that a data scientist must always document *why* they chose a specific treatment, as this is the moment where human judgment most heavily influences the final numbers.

tasks: Identify the percentage of missing values in each column of a provided dataset.
Compare the mean of a variable before and after mean imputation.
Discuss a scenario where dropping rows would introduce significant selection bias.

sessions.title: Duplicates and Outliers
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn how to detect redundant records and extreme values that can distort your statistical summaries. You will gain the ability to differentiate between 'bad' data and legitimate extreme observations using standard methods like the IQR rule. This ensures your subsequent modeling isn't skewed by errors or unique edge cases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that 'more data is always better' by introducing the concept of data pollution. Use the whiteboard to draw two simple bell curves: one clean, and one skewed significantly by a single extreme data point at the far right. Explain that while Unit 2 is about the 'unseen' 80% of data work, this specific session is about protecting the integrity of our signal. The core objective is to move beyond just deleting data and toward developing a 'statistical smell test'—learning to distinguish between a measurement error that must be purged and a rare, high-value insight that must be preserved.

Begin the technical discussion with Duplicates. On the whiteboard, illustrate the 'Identity Crisis' problem: two rows that share the same attributes but have different Primary Keys (UUIDs). Ask the students to consider a scenario in a retail database where a customer hits 'submit' twice on a slow connection. Explain the logic of checking for 'near-duplicates'—records that aren't identical in every column but are functionally the same. This leads into the first practice task: designing a logic check that ignores the ID column but looks for collisions in timestamps, user names, and transaction amounts. Emphasize that finding duplicates is easy, but deciding which one to keep requires a business rule (e.g., 'keep the first record' or 'merge the timestamps').

Transition to Outliers by returning to the bell curve. Introduce the Z-score as our first diagnostic tool for the 'Standard Normal' world. Draw a number line and mark the zero (mean) and units of standard deviation. Explain that a Z-score measures how many 'steps' a value is from the average. Mention the rule of thumb where values beyond ±3 standard deviations are often flagged. Warn students that the Z-score is sensitive to the very outliers it tries to find—because outliers pull the mean toward them, they can effectively 'hide' by inflating the standard deviation. This serves as a pivot to why we need more robust tools.

Introduce the Interquartile Range (IQR) and the Box Plot as the robust alternative to the Z-score. Draw a Box Plot on the board, clearly labeling the Median, Q1 (25th percentile), and Q3 (75th percentile). Define the 'fences' as Q1 - 1.5*IQR and Q3 + 1.5*IQR. Explain why this is 'robust': the median and quartiles don't move just because one value is a million times larger than the rest. The goal here is to give students a visual framework for 'mathematical suspicion.' If a point falls outside these fences, it isn't automatically 'bad,' but it is officially 'interesting' and requires an investigation.

Conclude with the critical decision-making framework: To drop or not to drop? Use a case study approach, such as a dataset of human heights where one entry is '250 cm' (plausible but rare) versus '2500 cm' (physically impossible). Explain that the former is a 'legitimate extreme' that might hold the key to a specific research question, while the latter is a 'data entry error.' Warn against the temptation of 'cherry-picking'—the dangerous habit of removing outliers simply because they make your model's R-squared look better. The final practice involves evaluating an outlier in context, forcing students to justify their choice based on the physics of the problem rather than just the math.

tasks: Use the Z-score method to flag potential outliers in a numerical series.
Write a logic check to find duplicate entries that have different primary keys but identical attributes.
Decide whether to keep or remove a specific outlier based on a provided case study.

sessions.title: Types, Units, and Encodings
sessions.description: This session focuses on the technical consistency of data, covering date formats, currency units, and character encoding issues. You will learn to standardize disparate data formats into a unified representation suitable for computation. This is a foundational step that prevents silent errors in mathematical operations and ensures cross-dataset compatibility.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by presenting a simple mathematical problem: adding two numbers. However, visually demonstrate on the board that if one '100' represents 100 USD and the other '100' represents 100 EUR, the sum is not 200. This opens the discussion on 'Silent Errors.' Explain that while a computer sees a floating-point number, the data scientist must see the metadata—the context of types and units. The core message of this session is that data is meaningless without standardized representation, and technical consistency is the prerequisite for any valid mathematical operation.

Introduce the concept of Data Types through the lens of memory and logic. Draw a distinction between 'Strings' (text used for labels) and 'Numerics' (values used for calculation). A common pitfall for beginners is treating categorical IDs, like ZIP codes, as numbers; explain why calculating the 'average ZIP code' is a logical fallacy. Transition to Date and Time formats, which are the most notorious source of frustration. Use a whiteboard timeline to show how '01/02/2023' is ambiguous—is it January 2nd or February 1st? Introduce ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) as the 'universal language' of data science and emphasize that converting to a proper datetime object unlocks time-series capabilities that simple strings cannot provide.

Shift the focus to the 'Unit Problem' in multi-source datasets. Use an example of a global retail company merging sales data from different regions. If the columns are just labeled 'Price,' the analysis will be fundamentally flawed. Illustrate a normalization workflow: identify the source currency, fetch a fixed exchange rate, and create a new standardized column. This prevents the bias that occurs when large numbers in one unit (like Yen) dwarf smaller numbers in another (like Pounds), purely because of the scale rather than the value.

Address the 'hidden' layer of data: Character Encoding. Explain that when a computer opens a file, it uses a 'decoder ring' like UTF-8 or ASCII. If the wrong ring is used, we get 'mojibake' or broken symbols. Sketch out a scenario where a CSV file from an older system appears garbled. Teach the students to treat this as a translation error rather than a data loss issue. This demystifies the 'UnicodeDecodeError' that often stops novices in their tracks, reframing it as a simple configuration mismatch to be solved before cleaning begins.

Conclude with a practice moment focused on 'Defensive Typing.' Ask the students to look at a list of mixed date formats and identify which ones would break a standard parser. The goal here is to build an intuition for 'edge cases'—the one record out of ten thousand that uses a different slash or a different currency symbol. This session ties back to the overarching goal of the unit: ensuring that when we finally run our models, we are comparing apples to apples, not apples to oranges or strings.

tasks: Convert a list of strings containing mixed date formats into a standard datetime object.
Normalize a column of prices where some are in USD and others in EUR using a fixed exchange rate.
Fix a 'broken' text file by identifying the correct character encoding.

sessions.title: Data Validation
sessions.description: This session introduces the concept of automated data quality checks and sanity testing. You will learn how to write assertions and validation rules to ensure data adheres to business logic and physical constraints. This builds the habit of 'defensive data science,' ensuring that your analysis pipeline breaks loudly if the input data changes unexpectedly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin by introducing the philosophy of 'Defensive Data Science.' Much like defensive driving, where you anticipate hazards before they occur, defensive data science assumes that your data source is inherently volatile and prone to breaking. Explain that until now, we have been manually looking for missing values or outliers. However, in a professional pipeline, you cannot manually inspect every new batch of data. The core concept here is the 'Loud Failure': it is far better for a script to crash immediately when it encounters impossible data (like a negative age) than for it to silently calculate an incorrect average that leads to a million-dollar business error. Draw a contrast on the board between a 'silent error' pipeline and a 'validated' pipeline to show how validation acts as a gatekeeper.

Transition into the mechanics of Schema and Type Validation. Explain that a validation rule is essentially a formalization of our assumptions. If we assume a column named 'Age' contains integers, we must encode that assumption into an assertion. Use the board to sketch out a simple 'Expectation' framework. For example, 'I expect this column to be non-null,' 'I expect these values to fall between 0 and 120,' and 'I expect this string to match a specific regex pattern.' The most important idea here is that validation is the bridge between business logic—the human understanding of what is possible—and the raw bits in the computer. A common pitfall for students is writing rules that are too rigid, such as expecting exactly 100 rows every day; guide them toward thinking in terms of ranges and logical constraints instead.

Introduce the concept of Multi-field or Relational Validation. This moves beyond checking a single column to checking the logic between columns. Use the 'Start Date vs. End Date' example. On the board, show how a record might pass individual checks (both are valid dates) but fail the logical check (the end date is in 1990 while the start date is in 2023). This highlights that data quality isn't just about 'clean' values, but 'coherent' stories. Explain that this type of validation often catches 'upstream' system bugs, where two different databases were merged incorrectly. This empowers the data scientist to not just clean data, but to diagnose systemic issues in the organization's data infrastructure.

Conclude by discussing the 'Validation Report' as a deliverable. Instead of just stopping the code, a sophisticated system should generate a diagnostic summary. Illustrate a report structure on the board that categorizes errors: 'Critical' (stop the pipeline) vs. 'Warning' (log the error but proceed). This teaches students how to manage the trade-off between data purity and operational continuity. For the final practice, have them design a summary report for five checks. This exercise isn't just about writing code; it’s about deciding which violations are deal-breakers and which are merely 'messy.' This shifts their mindset from a student following instructions to a gatekeeper of data integrity who must make high-stakes calls on data quality.

tasks: Create a validation rule to ensure an 'Age' column only contains values between 0 and 120.
Write a script to check that the 'Start Date' is always before the 'End Date' in a project tracking dataset.
Design a summary report that flags any records failing a set of five validation checks.

lectures.title: Transformation
lectures.description: This lecture covers the 'verbs' of data manipulation, teaching you how to reshape and combine data to prepare it for advanced analysis and visualization.

sessions.title: Filtering and Selecting
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to subset data efficiently based on complex logical conditions. You will learn to isolate the specific rows and columns needed for a particular question, reducing noise and computational overhead. This skill is essential for focusing your analysis on the most relevant subsets of large datasets.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by conceptualizing a dataset not as a fixed file, but as a vast marble block from which we must carve out the relevant information. Explain that 'Filtering' and 'Selecting' are the primary chisels of the data scientist. The central goal here is to shift students from a 'see everything' spreadsheet mindset to a 'query-based' programmatic mindset. Begin by drawing a simple rectangular grid on the board. Use horizontal sweeps to represent 'Filtering' (rows/observations) and vertical strokes to represent 'Selecting' (columns/variables). It is critical to emphasize that reducing the data size isn't just about speed; it's about reducing cognitive load so we can answer specific questions without the noise of irrelevant data.

Transition into the logic of Selection. Focus on the concept of 'Feature Subset Selection.' Explain that in real-world datasets, you might have hundreds of columns, but only three or four contribute to your specific hypothesis. Illustrate this by drawing a 'wide' table with columns like UserID, Sales, Region, Timestamp, BrowserType, and IPAddress. If our question is 'What is the regional performance?', we must justify why we drop the IPAddress and BrowserType—not because they are bad data, but because they are irrelevant for this specific lens. This introduces the idea of memory efficiency; explain that loading only the columns you need can be the difference between a script that runs in seconds and one that crashes your computer.

Move to the logic of Filtering, which is often more complex because it relies on Boolean logic. Use the 'Sales > $10,000 and Region = West' example to introduce the concept of the 'Mask' or 'Filter Vector.' On the whiteboard, show how a condition is applied to every single row, returning a list of True/False values. This is a foundational bridge: students must understand that the software doesn't just 'find' the rows; it evaluates a logical statement for every entry. Warn them about the common pitfall of 'Inclusive vs. Exclusive' boundaries—for instance, when filtering for the 'last 30 days,' does that include today? Does it include exactly 30 days ago at midnight? These small logical gaps are where most data errors occur.

Introduce a mini-practice moment by asking students to define the logic for finding 'loyal but inactive' users. This exercise is designed to reveal if they can combine multiple conditions—such as (SignupDate < 1 year ago) AND (LastLogin > 6 months ago). This forces them to think about the intersection of sets. Use the whiteboard to draw a Venn diagram showing where these logical conditions overlap. This visual helps students realize that filtering is essentially the act of defining the boundaries of a specific sub-population they want to study.

Conclude by discussing the 'Drop' operation as the inverse of selection. Sometimes it is easier to say what we *don't* want than what we *do* want. Explain the 'inplace' vs. 'copy' distinction—a classic trap for beginners. If you filter data but don't save it to a new variable, the 'marble block' remains uncarved. Emphasize that every transformation should be intentional and documented, as this is the first step toward building a reproducible data pipeline.

tasks: Select all rows where 'Sales' are greater than $10,000 and 'Region' is 'West'.
Filter a dataset to include only users who signed up in the last 30 days.
Drop unnecessary columns from a wide dataset to improve memory efficiency.

sessions.title: Grouping and Aggregating
sessions.description: This session introduces the Split-Apply-Combine paradigm for summarizing data at different scales. You will learn how to calculate group-level statistics like means, counts, and sums to compare different categories. This is the primary way data scientists uncover trends and variations across different segments of a population.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a massive, disorganized cloud of data points on the board representing every single transaction in a global retail company. The key idea to communicate here is that data in its raw, granular form is often too 'noisy' to inform decisions. We need to move from the individual level to the collective level. This transition is managed by the 'Split-Apply-Combine' paradigm—a phrase that should be written in large letters at the top of the board. Explain that this isn't just a technical trick, but a fundamental way of thinking: we break a big, messy problem into smaller, homogenous groups, solve for each group, and then stitch the results back together into a meaningful summary.

Begin the first phase of the 'Split' by visualizing a single table being sliced into sub-tables based on a shared characteristic, such as 'Product Category.' It is vital to emphasize that the 'key' used for splitting must be categorical. A common pitfall for beginners is trying to group by a continuous variable like 'Price,' which leads to thousands of groups with one item each. Use a quick verbal check: ask the students if grouping by 'Exact Timestamp' makes sense for finding daily trends. This helps them realize they must often 'bucket' or 'bin' data before they can successfully split it.

Once the groups are separated, move to the 'Apply' phase. On the board, draw different operations being performed on these mini-tables. This is where we define 'Aggregation.' Distinguish between functions that reduce a list of numbers to a single value (like Sum, Mean, or Max) versus transformations. The 'aha!' moment here should be that aggregation is a lossy process—we are intentionally throwing away individual details to gain a 'bird's-eye view.' Use the 'average revenue per category' task to illustrate this: we no longer care about who bought the item or at what time; we only care about the collective performance of 'Electronics' vs. 'Furniture.'

Progress to the 'Combine' phase by showing the individual results merging back into a new, smaller, and cleaner table. This is the output that stakeholders actually want to see. Introduce the concept of multi-aggregation here—calculating the Min, Max, and Mean simultaneously. Explain that looking at the Mean alone can be deceptive; if the Max is an extreme outlier, the 'average' might not represent a typical day. By showing multiple stats side-by-side, we give the data 'texture' and 'context.' This is a perfect moment for a practice check: have the students consider a 10-year weather dataset and ask why we would want the Max temperature per month rather than the Mean. The goal is to get them thinking about the specific business or scientific question (e.g., 'What is the worst-case heatwave?') rather than just clicking buttons.

Wrap up the session by addressing the 'Index' issue that often confuses students in programming libraries. When we group by 'Region,' that region name often moves from being a data column to a 'label' for the row. Use a whiteboard diagram to show how a table's shape fundamentally changes after aggregation: it becomes shorter and more focused. Warn them that after grouping, they cannot easily access individual row data anymore because those rows have been 'collapsed.' This reinforces the idea that Grouping and Aggregating is a one-way bridge toward higher-level synthesis, preparing them for the next step of joining these summaries with other datasets.

tasks: Calculate the average revenue per product category.
Find the maximum daily temperature for each month in a 10-year weather dataset.
Use multiple aggregation functions (min, max, mean) on a single grouped object.

sessions.title: Joining Datasets
sessions.description: This session covers the mechanics of merging data from multiple sources using keys, similar to SQL joins. You will understand the differences between inner, outer, left, and right joins and when to use each. This allows you to enrich your primary dataset with external information, such as adding demographic data to transaction logs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by drawing two distinct shapes on the whiteboard—perhaps a circle representing 'Customers' and a square representing 'Transactions.' The fundamental challenge of data science is that the world doesn't hand us a single unified table; it gives us fragments. We begin by defining the 'Primary Key' and 'Foreign Key' not as abstract database terms, but as the 'connective tissue' that allows us to tell a complete story. Use a simple analogy of a coat check: the ticket in your hand (Foreign Key) must match the ticket on the coat (Primary Key) to retrieve your belongings. This conceptual grounding is vital for ensuring students understand that joining is about matching identities, not just stacking rows.

Transition into the four primary join types by drawing a Venn diagram—the classic visualization tool for set theory. Start with the 'Inner Join.' Explain that this is the most restrictive and safest operation, as it only keeps the records where both sides agree. On the board, illustrate a scenario where an order exists but the customer ID is missing from the master list; in an inner join, that order vanishes. This leads naturally to the most common trap for beginners: 'data loss.' Explain that if they use an inner join by default, they might accidentally delete 20% of their business activity just because of a typo in a key. This realization helps them appreciate why we need more nuanced tools.

Now, introduce the 'Left Join' as the workhorse of data science. Illustrate this by keeping all the 'Circles' (Customers) and only pulling in 'Squares' (Transactions) that match. Emphasize that the 'Left' side is the anchor—it represents the population you care about. If a customer hasn't bought anything, they still stay in the table, but their transaction data is 'NULL.' This is a critical teaching moment: 'NULL' is not an error; it is information. It tells us which customers are inactive. Contrast this with the 'Right Join' and the 'Full Outer Join,' explaining that while they exist, we usually prefer to re-order our logic to stay in a Left-Join mindset for consistency and readability.

Move to the 'One-to-Many' relationship, which is where the most dangerous logic errors occur. Draw one customer linked to three different orders. Show how the customer's demographic data—like their age or city—gets duplicated for every order row. This 'fan-out' effect can lead to disastrously incorrect calculations, such as summing the customer's age and getting a number three times higher than reality. Teach students to always check their row counts before and after a join. If the table suddenly grew by 10,000 rows, they need to know if that was intended or if they just accidentally created a Cartesian product by joining on a non-unique key.

Conclude with a practice walkthrough focused on 'messy keys.' Present a scenario where 'Employee ID' is '001' in one table but just '1' in another. Use the whiteboard to show that computer logic is literal; these won't match. This reinforces the need for the cleaning skills learned in the previous session (string manipulation) before the join can happen. The final takeaway should be that joining is a deliberate act of reconstruction: you are building a larger truth by carefully stitching together smaller, reliable facts.

tasks: Perform a left join to attach employee names to a list of department IDs.
Identify which records are lost during an inner join of two messy tables.
Resolve 'duplicate key' issues when merging two datasets with a one-to-many relationship.

sessions.title: Reshaping: Wide and Long
sessions.description: This session explains the concepts of 'tidy' data and how to pivot between wide and long formats. You will learn why long formats are often preferred for visualization and modeling and how to convert them back for reporting. This flexibility is key to using modern data science libraries that expect specific data structures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by drawing a typical 'spreadsheet' on the board: columns for 2021, 2022, and 2023 sales, with product names as rows. This is the 'Wide' format we naturally use in Excel. Explain that while this is easy for humans to read and compare years at a glance, it is a nightmare for computers. The core concept to establish here is the 'Variable vs. Observation' distinction. In this wide table, the variable 'Year' is actually scattered across three different column headers, and the variable 'Sales' is the values within them. This breaks the fundamental rule of 'Tidy Data': each variable must have its own column.

Transition to the 'Long' format by literally redrawing that table. Show how we collapse those year columns into a single 'Year' column and a single 'Value' column. Use the term 'Melting' or 'Unpivoting' to describe this act of stretching the data vertically. The most important idea to convey here is that computers (and modern visualization libraries like ggplot2 or Plotly) are 'column-hungry'—they need to see a column named 'Year' so they can map it to an X-axis or a color aesthetic. A common student misconception is that long data is redundant because the product names repeat; clarify that this repetition is the necessary cost of making the data machine-readable.

Now, introduce the 'Pivot' as the reverse operation. Ask the class: 'If Long is so great for analysis, why do we ever go back to Wide?' Use a cross-tabulation example, like a frequency count of sales by 'Region' and 'Product Category.' Explain that for a final executive report or a printed summary table, humans need to see a matrix to spot patterns quickly. This illustrates that data transformation isn't about finding the 'perfect' shape, but about choosing the right shape for the current task—modeling/plotting (Long) vs. presentation/summarization (Wide).

Walk through a mental exercise: if we wanted to create a time-series line chart, which format would we use? Guide them to see that in a wide format, the computer doesn't know '2021' and '2022' are the same kind of thing (Time); it just sees two unrelated columns. In a long format, 'Year' becomes a continuous dimension. Finally, warn about the 'messy middle'—datasets where some columns are already tidy and others are wide. Emphasize that the first step in any real-world project is identifying which columns are 'ID variables' (the things that stay the same) and which are 'Measure variables' (the things being collapsed).

tasks: Melt a wide table of yearly sales into a long format with 'Year' and 'Amount' columns.
Pivot a long-format dataset to create a cross-tabulation of two categorical variables.
Explain which format is better for creating a time-series line chart.

lectures.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on the 'detective work' of data science, using descriptive statistics and relationship analysis to generate hypotheses and uncover hidden truths.

sessions.title: Distributions and Summary Statistics
sessions.description: This session moves beyond simple means to look at the shape of data through medians, variance, and percentiles. You will learn to recognize normal, skewed, and multimodal distributions and what they tell you about the underlying process. This provides the context necessary to determine if a 'typical' value is actually representative of the whole.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common instinct to summarize a complex dataset with a single number. While everyone knows how to calculate an average, explain that the 'mean' is often a trap in data science. Draw a simple horizontal line representing a distribution of wealth: on one end, nine people with $10, and on the other, one person with $1,000. Show how the mean suggests an 'average' wealth of $109, which describes absolutely no one in the room. This illustrates the central theme of today’s lecture: summary statistics are not the data itself; they are lossy compressions that can lie if we don't understand the 'shape' or distribution of the underlying values.

Transition to the visual representation of data by drawing three distinct histogram shapes: the Bell Curve (Normal), the Skewed Tail, and the Two-Humped Camel (Bimodal). Explain that the shape of the data tells the story of the process that created it. A normal distribution suggests a process governed by many small, independent random factors, like human heights. A skewed distribution, however, points to 'winner-take-all' mechanics or physical limits, such as income or reaction times. Crucially, show where the Mean, Median, and Mode sit on a skewed graph. When the mean is pulled far away from the median toward the tail, it’s a signal that outliers are exerting a disproportionate influence, and as a data scientist, you must decide which measure of 'centrality' actually serves your business question.

Introduce the concept of 'spread' using percentiles and the Interquartile Range (IQR). Instead of just giving the formula for variance, visualize it as the 'vibrancy' or 'uncertainty' of the data points around the center. Draw a box plot alongside a histogram to show how the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles slice the data into four equal-sized groups of people, regardless of the values themselves. This helps learners move from thinking about 'scores' to thinking about 'rankings.' Explain that the middle 50% (the IQR) is the most honest representation of a dataset’s core behavior because it ignores the 'noise' of extreme outliers that would otherwise inflate the standard deviation.

Lead the students into a practice moment by presenting a bimodal distribution—two peaks separated by a valley. Ask them to hypothesize why a dataset of 'delivery times' for a restaurant might show two distinct humps. The goal here is to get them to realize that a bimodal distribution usually means you are looking at two different populations accidentally mixed together—perhaps 'weekday lunch' vs. 'weekend dinner.' This realization is vital: before you calculate a mean or a median, you must first ask if the data is coming from a single, unified source, or if you need to segment your data before analyzing it.

Conclude by reinforcing that 'Typical' is a relative term. Summarize the logic chain: first, look at the histogram to see the shape; second, check for symmetry to decide between mean and median; and third, use percentiles to understand the boundaries of the 'normal' experience. Warn against the common mistake of applying 'Normal Distribution' assumptions (like the 68-95-99.7 rule) to skewed data. By the end of this session, students should feel that looking at a single average without seeing the distribution is like looking at a map with the North Star but no landmarks—you know a direction, but you have no idea where you actually are.

tasks: Compare the mean and median of a highly skewed income distribution.
Calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles to determine the range of the middle 50%.
Identify if a provided histogram suggests a bimodal distribution and hypothesize why.

sessions.title: Comparing Groups
sessions.description: This session focuses on visual and numerical comparisons between different categories in your data. You will learn to use box plots and grouped summaries to see if differences between groups are substantial or likely due to chance. This is the first step toward building predictive models that use categorical features to explain variance.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the instinct to only look at averages. While the previous session established how to describe a single group, real data science begins when we ask, 'Is Group A actually different from Group B?' Use a relatable scenario, such as comparing the effectiveness of two different teaching methods or the spending habits of two customer segments. The goal here is to shift students' focus from 'what is the number?' to 'what is the difference?' and to help them understand that a difference in means is meaningless without understanding the spread surrounding those means.

Introduce the Box Plot as the primary visual tool for this detective work. On the whiteboard, draw a standard box plot and explain its components not as statistical definitions, but as physical markers of data density. Show how the 'box' represents the middle 50% of the population, emphasizing that if two boxes do not overlap, we have strong visual evidence of a fundamental difference. Contrast this with a scenario where the means are different but the boxes overlap significantly, explaining that in such cases, the 'difference' might just be noise or random chance. This visual intuition is a crucial precursor to formal hypothesis testing they will encounter later in the course.

Transition into the concept of variability or 'spread' as the hidden story within the data. Use the example of two groups with the same average test score: one group where everyone scored 75, and another where half scored 100 and half scored 50. Use the whiteboard to sketch these distributions. Explain that the Standard Deviation is our numerical tool for measuring this 'volatility.' A key pedagogical point here is to warn students against the 'Average Trap'—assuming a group is monolithic. Teaching them to look for the group with the highest variability helps them identify where a process is inconsistent or where a customer segment might actually be composed of two hidden sub-types.

Conduct a practice moment where students compare three distinct customer segments. Ask them to look at a provided set of box plots and identify not just which group spends the most, but which group is the most 'predictable.' This exercise is designed to reveal if students can connect low variability to high predictability. If they only focus on the median, redirect them to the length of the whiskers and the size of the box, explaining that a wide box represents uncertainty, which is a data scientist's greatest enemy when building predictive models.

Conclude by framing this group comparison as the 'first step toward modeling.' Explain that when we find a categorical variable (like 'Teaching Method' or 'Region') that clearly separates our data into different distributions, we have found a 'feature.' This sets the stage for Unit 4, where they will learn to use these features to build mathematical models. End with a cautionary note: just because groups look different doesn't mean the category *caused* the difference—a nudge toward the next session on Correlation and the eventual discussion on Simpson's Paradox.

tasks: Compare the distribution of test scores between two different teaching methods using box plots.
Identify which group has the highest variability (standard deviation) in a performance dataset.
Draft a short observation about the differences found between three customer segments.

sessions.title: Relationships and Correlation
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn to quantify the strength and direction of the relationship between two numerical variables using Pearson’s correlation. You will gain the ability to interpret scatter plots and correlation coefficients ranging from -1 to 1. This helps you identify which variables might be useful predictors for your future models.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by drawing a simple scatter plot on the whiteboard. Place 'Advertising Spend' on the horizontal axis and 'Units Sold' on the vertical axis. The primary goal of this opening is to transition the class from looking at one variable in isolation (distributions) to seeing how two variables 'dance' together. Explain that while distributions tell us about a population's state, relationships tell us about its mechanics. Draw a cloud of points that generally trends upward and ask the students what they see. This visual intuition—that as one thing goes up, another usually follows—is the 'why' behind correlation. It’s the first step in predictive modeling: finding a signal that allows us to guess the value of Y if we only know X.

Now, introduce the Pearson Correlation Coefficient ($r$) as the mathematical tool that turns this visual 'vibe' into a precise number between -1 and +1. Use the whiteboard to illustrate the three benchmark cases: +1 (a perfect line up), -1 (a perfect line down), and 0 (a chaotic cloud). It is vital to emphasize that the sign (+ or -) indicates direction, while the absolute value indicates strength. A common mistake students make is thinking that -0.8 is 'less' than 0.2 because it is a negative number; clarify that -0.8 is actually a much stronger, more reliable relationship. Use the 'Advertising' example to show a positive relationship, then pivot to something like 'Price' vs. 'Units Sold' to demonstrate a negative relationship, helping them internalize that negative correlation is just as useful for prediction.

Transition to the concept of 'linearity' by drawing a U-shaped curve or a circle of points. Here, ask the students to estimate the correlation. Most will struggle. Reveal that the Pearson correlation for these shapes is often near zero. This is a critical teaching moment: $r$ only measures linear relationships. If the relationship is a curve, the math 'gets confused' and tells you there is no relationship at all, even though the pattern is obvious to the human eye. This warns learners never to trust a correlation coefficient without first looking at the scatter plot. It prevents them from missing complex, non-linear insights in their future data projects.

Introduce a brief practice moment where students calculate a simplified correlation coefficient or rank different scatter plots by their $r$ values. During this, walk around and look for students who confuse the slope of the line with the strength of the correlation. Address this by drawing two lines: one very steep and one very shallow, but both perfectly straight. Explain that both have a correlation of 1.0. Correlation doesn't care about the 'steepness' (the beta coefficient in regression), it only cares about how tightly the points hug the line. This distinction is the bridge they will need for Unit 4 when they learn formal regression.

Conclude by framing correlation as a 'search tool' for feature engineering. Explain that in a real dataset with 100 variables, we use a correlation matrix to quickly highlight which variables might be the best 'leads' for further investigation. However, leave them with a cautionary note that high correlation does not mean one variable causes the other—it simply means they move in sync. This sets the stage for the next session on Simpson’s Paradox, where we will see how these seemingly strong relationships can be misleading if we don't account for hidden factors.

tasks: Calculate the correlation coefficient between 'Advertising Spend' and 'Units Sold'.
Identify a non-linear relationship in a scatter plot where the correlation coefficient is near zero.
Explain the difference between a correlation of 0.8 and -0.8.

sessions.title: Confounding and Simpson's Paradox
sessions.description: This session warns against jumping to conclusions by introducing the concept of confounding variables and Simpson's Paradox. You will see how a trend appearing in different groups of data can disappear or reverse when these groups are combined. This critical thinking skill prevents you from making defenseless claims and prepares you for the 'Causality vs Correlation' discussion in Unit 5.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the natural human tendency to seek easy causal links. This is the 'detective's caution' phase of the lecture. Begin on the whiteboard by drawing two parallel trends: rising ice cream sales and rising shark attacks. Ask the students if eating ice cream causes shark attacks. This humorous, classic example immediately introduces the concept of a 'Confounding Variable'—in this case, temperature or summer season—which influences both observed variables. The core idea here is to instill a healthy skepticism: just because two things move together (correlation) does not mean one drives the other. This prevents the common pitfall of assuming that every statistical relationship is actionable.

Transition into the more counterintuitive and mathematically startling phenomenon of Simpson’s Paradox. Use the whiteboard to present a scenario where a medical treatment appears more effective for 'Group A' and more effective for 'Group B' individually, but appears less effective when the data is pooled. This is the moment to emphasize that the 'whole' is not always a simple sum of its parts. Explain the logic: the 'hidden' variable (perhaps the severity of the illness) is distributed unevenly across the treatment groups. The most important takeaway is that aggregated data can hide, or even flip, the underlying truth, making it dangerous to make high-stakes decisions based solely on top-line numbers.

Deepen the intuition by walking through the UC Berkeley admissions case study. On the whiteboard, show the overall admission rates which suggest a bias against one gender. Then, break the data down by department. Students will see that within individual departments, the bias often disappears or even favors the previously 'disadvantaged' group. Explain that the 'confounder' here is the choice of department—one gender tended to apply to more competitive departments with lower acceptance rates overall. This exercise is designed to reveal how 'looking under the hood' of a dataset through segmentation isn't just a technical step, but an ethical necessity in data science.

Conclude the session with a practical framework for 'defensive analysis.' Teach students to always ask: 'What are we not seeing?' and 'Is there a sub-group that behaves differently?' Introduce the technique of data segmentation as the primary defense against Simpson's Paradox. The final practice moment should involve students proposing how to segment a generic 'productivity' dataset (e.g., remote vs. in-office work) to ensure they aren't missing a confounding factor like job role or seniority. This prepares them for the more formal causal inference and bias discussions in later units by framing data science as an ongoing process of uncovering hidden layers of context.

tasks: Analyze a classic dataset (like the UC Berkeley admissions case) to identify Simpson's Paradox.
Identify a potential third variable that might confound the relationship between ice cream sales and shark attacks.
Propose a way to segment a dataset to check for hidden trends.

projects.deliverable_increment: A 'Cleaned Dataset' file and a collection of 'Exploratory Plots' (histograms and scatter plots) showing data distributions and correlations.

exams.title: Cleaning and Exploratory Data Analysis Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the student's ability to transform messy raw data into a clean, structured format and identify significant statistical patterns and potential pitfalls in the results.
