units.title: Inference and Modeling
units.description: Move beyond description into prediction and inference. This unit introduces the statistical foundations required to test hypotheses and build regression and classification models.

lectures.title: Statistical Thinking
lectures.description: This lecture transitions from descriptive summaries to formal statistical inference, establishing how we can draw reliable conclusions about large populations from limited sample data.

sessions.title: Populations, Samples, and Randomness
sessions.description: This session introduces the fundamental distinction between a population parameter and a sample statistic, explaining why random sampling is the bedrock of valid inference. You will learn to identify different sampling strategies and the role of randomness in reducing selection bias. This conceptual foundation is critical for ensuring that any subsequent modeling you perform is actually representative of the real world.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that 'more data' is always 'better data.' In a concept-first public lecture style, begin by drawing a massive, amorphous cloud on the whiteboard labeled 'The Population.' Explain that this represents the totality of what we care about—every customer in a market, every heartbeat in a lifetime, or every grain of sand on a beach. Immediately contrast this with a tiny, distinct circle labeled 'The Sample.' The goal is to move from the chaotic, unreachable truth of the population (parameters) to the manageable, observable evidence of the sample (statistics). The logic to emphasize here is that in data science, we are almost always 'looking through a keyhole'—the sample—to describe a room we cannot enter—the population.

Deepen the distinction by introducing the Greek vs. Latin notation on the board: write μ (mu) and σ (sigma) inside the population cloud and x̄ (x-bar) and s next to the sample circle. Explain that while we calculate the sample mean to estimate the population mean, they are fundamentally different species: one is a fixed but unknown truth, and the other is a fluctuating, observable estimate. This is the moment to address the 'Certainty Trap'—the mistake of assuming that because we have calculated a number from our data, it is the absolute truth for the whole group. We must treat our sample results with a level of humility, recognizing them as estimates subject to change.

Transition into the 'How' of sampling by discussing the mechanism of the Random Sample. Use the metaphor of a well-stirred soup: you don't need to eat the whole pot to know if it's too salty, provided the soup was stirred properly. On the board, illustrate 'Selection Bias' by drawing a sample circle that only pulls from one corner of the population cloud. Ask the students: 'If I only survey people entering a luxury gym about their health, can I describe the health of the city?' This reveals the danger of non-randomness—it creates a systematic 'tilt' in our results that no amount of fancy math can fix later. Emphasize that randomness is our insurance policy against our own hidden biases.

Now, introduce the practice task where students evaluate research scenarios. The intention here is to force them to identify the 'Invisible Population.' For example, in a marketing survey sent via email, the population isn't just 'customers,' but perhaps 'active, tech-savvy customers who open emails.' This exercise is designed to reveal how easily we accidentally redefine our population based on who is easiest to reach. Guide them to see that the gap between who we *want* to study and who we *actually* study is where most data science projects fail.

Conclude by framing 'Inference' as a bridge. The rest of this unit will be about building that bridge, but today we are ensuring the foundation—the sampling method—is solid. Warn them that if the bridge is built on a biased sample, it doesn't matter how beautiful the architecture is; it will lead to the wrong destination. This sets the stage for the next session on sampling distributions, moving from the 'Who' of sampling to the 'How often' of the results.

tasks: Identify the population and sample in three different research scenarios.
Explain how a non-random sampling method could lead to biased conclusions in a marketing survey.

sessions.title: Sampling Distributions
sessions.description: This session explores the concept of a sampling distribution and the Central Limit Theorem through visual intuition. You will discover how the means of many samples follow a normal distribution even if the original data does not. Understanding this 'regularity in randomness' is the essential bridge that allows us to calculate the probability of our observations and justifies the use of common statistical tests.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by addressing the fundamental anxiety of statistics: the fear that our small sample is just an unlucky fluke. While the previous session established the difference between populations and samples, this session reveals the 'magic' that makes inference possible. Begin the whiteboard session by drawing a highly irregular, perhaps bimodal or heavily skewed distribution (e.g., household income or the number of likes on social media posts). This 'parent population' represents the messy reality we usually can't see in its entirety. The goal is to show that while individual data points are chaotic, the behavior of 'groups'—specifically the means of those groups—is remarkably predictable. This sets the stage for the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) not as a dry formula, but as a law of nature.

Illustrate the process of repeated sampling. Draw three small circles representing three different samples of size n=5. Calculate the average of each circle and plot those three averages on a new, separate axis below the original distribution. Then, imagine doing this 10,000 times. As you draw the resulting curve for these averages, emphasize that this new shape is the 'Sampling Distribution.' The most important realization for the student here is that this new distribution of means is much narrower and more symmetric than the parent population. You are teaching them that while an individual person might be an outlier, the average of 100 people is rarely an outlier. This 'regularity in randomness' is the bridge we need to cross to reach probability.

Introduce the Central Limit Theorem formally through this visualization. Explain that as the sample size (n) increases, three things happen: the center of the sampling distribution stays at the population mean, the shape becomes more Bell-shaped (Normal), and the spread (variation) shrinks. Use the whiteboard to derive the concept of 'Standard Error' by comparing a sample size of n=5 versus n=100. Visually show that the curve for n=100 is much taller and thinner. This is a critical moment to clarify a common misconception: students often confuse the standard deviation of the population with the standard error of the mean. Explain that the standard error is simply the standard deviation of our 'imaginary' distribution of averages, representing how much we expect our sample mean to jump around if we repeated the experiment.

Transition to a practical exercise to test these intuitions. Ask students to sketch what the sampling distribution would look like for a sample size of n=2 versus n=50 for the skewed population drawn earlier. The goal of this exercise is to reveal if they understand that 'Normalizing' takes time and data; a sample of 2 will still look skewed, while 50 will look like a Bell curve. Follow this with a calculation of the standard error using the formula (sigma / sqrt(n)). Use a simple example, like a population standard deviation of 20. Contrast the error for n=4 (error=10) and n=100 (error=2). This calculation reveals the 'law of diminishing returns' in data collection: to cut your uncertainty in half, you often need to quadruple your data.

Conclude by tying this back to the data science lifecycle. Explain that the CLT is why we can use a sample mean to estimate a population mean with a measurable degree of confidence. It justifies why we can use Z-scores and Normal distribution tables even when our raw data is messy and non-normal. By the end of this session, students should no longer see a sample mean as a static number, but as a single point pulled from a beautiful, predictable Bell curve that exists in the background of every experiment they will ever run.

tasks: Sketch the expected sampling distribution of a mean for a highly skewed population as sample size increases.
Calculate the standard error given a population standard deviation and sample size.

sessions.title: Confidence Intervals
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to quantify uncertainty by constructing and interpreting confidence intervals for means and proportions. You will learn how to communicate the precision of an estimate rather than just providing a single 'point estimate.' This skill is vital for professional communication, as it prevents overconfidence in noisy data and provides a range of plausible values for decision-makers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the comfort of the 'point estimate.' Draw a single, sharp dot on the whiteboard representing a sample mean, like the average height of a group or the conversion rate of an ad. Explain that while this number is our best guess, presenting it in isolation is intellectually dishonest because it ignores the 'noise' we discussed in the previous session on sampling distributions. The goal of this session is to move from providing a single answer to providing a range of plausible values, shifting the conversation from 'what is the number?' to 'how much do we trust this number?'

Introduce the anatomy of a Confidence Interval (CI) by drawing a horizontal line with the point estimate in the center and 'arms' extending out to either side. Label these arms as the Margin of Error. This is the moment to bridge the math from the Central Limit Theorem: explain that because we know sample means cluster around the truth in a predictable bell curve, we can use the Standard Error as a ruler to measure out how far we need to reach to capture the true population parameter a certain percentage of the time. Use the whiteboard to show that a wider interval represents more uncertainty, while a narrower one represents higher precision.

Address the most common pitfall in all of statistics: the misinterpretation of the '95%'. Students often think it means there is a 95% chance the true value falls in the specific interval they just calculated. Explicitly correct this by explaining the frequentist perspective: the true value is a fixed (though unknown) constant, not a moving target. Our interval is the thing that moves. Use a visual of twenty different intervals stacked vertically; show that, on average, nineteen will 'trap' the true line and one will miss. This shifts the definition of confidence from a probability of a single result to a statement about the reliability of our process.

Walk through a live calculation for a sample mean, focusing on the trade-offs between confidence and precision. On the whiteboard, demonstrate what happens when we increase the confidence level from 90% to 99%—the interval must get wider to be 'more sure,' which makes the information less specific. Then, show how increasing the sample size (N) shrinks the standard error, pulling those arms in and giving us a tighter, more useful estimate. This illustrates the 'cost' of certainty and the power of larger data sets.

Conclude with a practice exercise using a political polling scenario. Ask the students to interpret a result like 'Support is 48% ± 3% at a 95% confidence level.' Guide them away from saying 'The candidate has a 95% chance of being at 48%' and toward the correct framing: 'We are 95% confident that the true population support lies between 45% and 51%.' This exercise is designed to reveal if they are still clinging to the 'probability' misconception or if they have internalised the idea of an interval as a tool for professional decision-making under uncertainty.

tasks: Interpret a 95% confidence interval for a political poll without using the word 'probability' incorrectly.
Calculate a confidence interval for a sample mean using a provided t-table or calculator.

sessions.title: Hypothesis Tests and p-Values
sessions.description: This session demystifies the logic of NHST (Null Hypothesis Statistical Testing), focusing on the correct interpretation of p-values and significance levels. You will learn to frame null and alternative hypotheses and determine when an observed effect is likely due to more than just chance. This is a core competency for any data scientist tasked with validating if a new product feature or treatment actually works.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by reframing the entire data science journey as a courtroom drama to ground the abstract logic of Null Hypothesis Statistical Testing (NHST). Start by drawing a 'Court of Science' on the board, where the accused is a 'New Observation' or 'Treatment Effect.' The fundamental concept to establish here is the Presumption of Innocence, which in our world is the Null Hypothesis ($H_0$). Explain that $H_0$ is the conservative baseline—the boring world where nothing special happened, the medicine doesn't work, and the website change didn't increase sales. Contrast this with the Alternative Hypothesis ($H_a$), which is the researcher's claim. The crucial takeaway for students must be that we never 'prove' $H_a$; we only gather enough evidence to make $H_0$ look so ridiculous that we are forced to reject it.

Transition to the mechanism of evidence by introducing the p-value through a 'World of Chance' visualization. Draw a distribution on the board representing the outcomes we would expect if only random noise were at play ($H_0$ is true). Mark a spot on the far tail representing our actual observed data. Define the p-value not as a complex formula, but as the probability of seeing data this extreme, or more extreme, if the Null Hypothesis were actually true. Use the example of a coin flip: if a coin comes up heads 10 times in a row, the p-value is the probability that a perfectly fair coin would do that. This setup helps prevent the most common student pitfall: thinking the p-value is the probability that the hypothesis is true or false. It is purely a measure of 'surprise' given a specific assumption.

Address the threshold of 'surprise' by introducing the significance level ($\alpha$). Draw a line on your distribution tail (typically at 0.05) to represent our 'Tolerance for Error.' Explain that $\alpha$ is our pre-set boundary for how much risk we are willing to take of being wrong when we claim a discovery. This is the moment to weave in a critical conceptual check: explain why a p-value of 0.04 does not mean there is a 96% chance the null is false. It simply means that if the null were true, we'd see this result only 4% of the time. Use this to highlight the 'False Positive' risk—if we set $\alpha$ to 0.05, we accept that in 1 out of 20 experiments where nothing is actually happening, we will mistakenly claim success. This connects the abstract math back to the business stakes of data-driven decisions.

Engage the students with a practical A/B testing scenario involving two website layouts. Ask them to frame the Null Hypothesis ($H_0$: Layout B has the same or lower conversion rate than Layout A) and the Alternative ($H_a$: Layout B is better). Use the whiteboard to map out how a small difference in conversion might result in a high p-value if the sample size is small (high noise), versus how that same difference becomes 'statistically significant' with a large sample (low noise). This exercise is designed to reveal if students are confusing the 'magnitude' of an effect with its 'certainty.'

Conclude by discussing the limitations of p-values in the real world. Introduce the idea that 'statistically significant' does not mean 'practically important.' A p-value of 0.001 might prove that a new button color increases clicks by 0.0001%, but the cost of the change might outweigh the benefit. This final beat ensures that the students leave not just with a mathematical tool, but with the professional judgment required to interpret that tool within a business or scientific context, rounding out the 'Concept-First' approach.

tasks: Define a null hypothesis for an A/B test comparing two website layouts.
Explain why a p-value of 0.04 does not mean there is a 96% chance the null hypothesis is false.

lectures.title: Regression
lectures.description: This lecture covers the most ubiquitous tool in the data scientist's toolkit: linear regression, focusing on modeling the relationship between variables and making continuous predictions.

sessions.title: Simple Linear Regression
sessions.description: This session introduces the 'line of best fit' and the method of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to model the relationship between one independent and one dependent variable. You will learn how to find the slope and intercept that minimize prediction error. This provides the fundamental building block for understanding how one variable influences another in a linear system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by grounding the session in a conceptual visualization rather than a formula. Draw a scatter plot of data points representing something intuitive, like years of experience versus annual salary. Explain that while the data points are scattered and messy, our human brain naturally tries to find a pattern or a 'trend line.' The primary goal of this session is to move from this fuzzy 'feeling' of a trend to a mathematically rigorous line that we can defend and use for predictions. This shift from intuition to calculation is the fundamental step in moving from basic observation to data science modeling.

Introduce the anatomy of the regression line: y = mx + b (or y = beta_0 + beta_1*x). On the whiteboard, draw a single point that does not sit on the line. Use a vertical dashed line to connect the point to the line, and label this gap as the 'residual' or error. This is a critical moment to clarify that we measure error vertically—the difference between the actual value and what the model predicted—not the shortest distance to the line. This prevents the common misconception that we are measuring perpendicular distance, which is a different type of modeling altogether. Explain that the 'best' line is the one where these vertical gaps, across all points, are as small as possible.

Transition into the logic of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). Pose a question: 'If we just sum up the residuals, will that tell us how bad our line is?' Demonstrate with two points—one above the line and one below—that a simple sum might result in zero, misleadingly suggesting a perfect fit because the positive and negative errors canceled out. This serves as the 'why' behind squaring the errors. By squaring them, every mistake becomes positive, and larger mistakes are penalized more heavily. On the whiteboard, illustrate this by drawing actual squares growing out of the residual lines; the goal of OLS is to find the line that makes the total area of all these squares as small as possible. This visual metaphor helps students internalize the 'Least Squares' terminology.

Introduce a brief manual exercise to solidify the concept of the residual. Give the students a simple line equation, such as y = 2x + 5, and an actual data point like (3, 15). Ask them to calculate the residual. This practice moment is designed to expose whether they understand that the 'prediction' comes from plugging 'x' into the formula, and the 'error' is the subtraction of that result from the actual 'y'. Once they've mastered the calculation, ask them to manually sketch five points on a coordinate plane and draw what they believe is the best-fit line. Have them estimate the slope by looking at the 'rise over run.' This builds a physical sense of the relationship before they ever touch a computer, ensuring they don't treat regression as a 'black box' button in a software package.

Conclude by discussing the limitations of a simple linear model. Mention that while we are finding the mathematical 'best' line, a line might still be a terrible fit if the underlying data is curved or contains extreme outliers. Explain that the slope tells us the 'rate of change'—how much we expect the target variable to move for every one-unit increase in our predictor. This sets the stage for the next session, where we will stop looking at just one influence and start considering the complex, multi-variable world using Multiple Regression.

tasks: Calculate the residual for a specific data point given a regression line equation.
Manually plot a best-fit line through a small set of five data points and estimate the slope.

sessions.title: Multiple Regression
sessions.description: This session extends the linear model to include multiple predictors, allowing you to account for several factors simultaneously. You will learn how to handle more complex real-world scenarios where a single outcome is influenced by many inputs. This session moves you closer to building professional-grade predictive models that reflect multi-dimensional reality.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the 'simple' line to the complexity of the real world. I’ll start by asking the students a conceptual question: if we want to predict the price of a house, does only the square footage matter? The immediate intuition is 'no'—location, age, and number of rooms matter too. This transition is vital because it moves the learner from a single-variable mindset to a multi-dimensional one. On the whiteboard, I will draw the familiar 2D regression line and then attempt to sketch a 3D plane, explaining that while we can't easily visualize four or five dimensions, the math scales effortlessly. The core idea here is that Multiple Regression isn't just 'more variables'; it's about isolating the unique contribution of each variable while holding others constant.

Next, I’ll tackle the concept of the 'Partial Coefficient,' which is perhaps the most critical conceptual hurdle in this session. I will use the example of ice cream sales, temperature, and drowning incidents to illustrate a classic 'spurious' relationship. By including both temperature and ice cream sales in a multiple regression to predict drownings, students will see that the coefficient for ice cream sales effectively drops to zero. I’ll explain that the model is now 'controlling' for temperature, allowing us to see the true (lack of) effect of ice cream. This distinction—moving from simple correlation to partial coefficients—is what makes Multiple Regression a tool for causal inference and decision science rather than just a simple trend-line tool. I want to prevent the common misconception that adding more variables always makes the individual coefficients more accurate; sometimes, it reveals that a previously 'significant' variable was just a bystander.

Following this, we move to the evaluation of model quality through R-squared. I will introduce the 'R-squared Trap.' On the board, I'll demonstrate that adding any variable—even one representing random noise or the number of birds in the sky—will mathematically never decrease the R-squared value. This is a crucial moment for a concept-first lecture: we must explain that R-squared only tells us about fit, not about the 'truth' or 'usefulness' of the model. I will hint at Adjusted R-squared as a penalty system, but the focus will remain on the logic: adding complexity always improves fit on training data, but it might just be 'modeling the noise.'

To wrap up, we will conduct a brief thought exercise. I’ll present a scenario where a model’s R-squared jumps from 0.6 to 0.8 after adding a new variable, but the coefficients of the original variables shift dramatically. I’ll ask the students to interpret what this shift means for the 'story' the data is telling. This exercise is designed to reveal whether they understand that variables in a multiple regression model are in a constant tug-of-war for 'credit' over the variance in the outcome. By the end of this session, students should view a regression model not as a static equation, but as a dynamic system where every included variable changes the context of every other variable.

tasks: Explain the difference between a simple correlation and a partial coefficient in a multiple regression model.
Determine how the addition of a new variable affects the R-squared value.

sessions.title: Interpreting Coefficients
sessions.description: This session focuses on the 'why' behind the model, teaching you how to translate mathematical weights into actionable business insights. You will learn how to explain to a stakeholder exactly what a one-unit increase in a predictor means for the target variable. Mastering interpretation ensures your data science work leads to defensible conclusions and clear recommendations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a bridge on the whiteboard, connecting a mathematical equation on one side to a boardroom decision on the other. Explain that while the previous sessions focused on 'finding' the line, this session is about 'speaking' for the line. Frame the regression coefficient not as a sterile number, but as a 'lever'—if we pull this lever by one unit, how much does the world change? This perspective is vital because stakeholders rarely care about the math; they care about the magnitude of impact and the direction of change. By positioning coefficients as actionable business levers, we move from being technical practitioners to strategic advisors.

Demonstrate the translation of the 'Unit-Change' rule using a concrete example, such as marketing spend versus revenue. Write the equation Y = 50 + 10X on the board. Explicitly contrast the mathematical jargon—'the slope of the independent variable'—with the professional interpretation: 'For every additional dollar we spend on ads, we expect to see an average increase of ten dollars in sales.' Emphasize the importance of the word 'average' and the phrase 'holding all other factors constant.' This is where many students trip up; they interpret regression as a deterministic law rather than a probabilistic trend. By hammering home the 'ceteris paribus' (all else equal) condition now, you prepare them for the complexities of multiple regression discussed previously.

Introduce the concept of 'Log-Transformed' variables by sketching a curve that flattens out, representing diminishing returns. This is a common real-world scenario (like the effect of experience on salary) that simple linear models miss. Show how a coefficient in a log-linear model changes from an absolute unit change to a percentage change. Explain that if we log the target variable, a coefficient of 0.05 means a 1-unit increase in X leads to approximately a 5% increase in Y. This distinction is the hallmark of a sophisticated analyst. Use a practice moment here: ask students to interpret a specific coefficient for a dummy variable (like 'Is_Weekend'), which forces them to realize that the 'unit' change is simply moving from a 'No' to a 'Yes' state.

Address the 'Correlation vs. Causation' trap within the context of interpretation. Warn the students that even if the coefficient is statistically significant and large, they must use cautious language like 'is associated with' rather than 'causes.' This prevents the common pitfall of over-promising results to management. Illustrate this by showing a regression of 'Ice Cream Sales' on 'Drowning Incidents.' The coefficient might be positive and high, but the 'lever' isn't real because the underlying factor is temperature. This part of the lecture is designed to build their professional ethics and skepticism, ensuring they don't just report numbers, but provide defensible narratives.

Conclude by challenging the students to synthesize these rules into a single sentence for a non-technical manager. The goal of the final practice task is to strip away the Greek letters (Alpha, Beta, Epsilon) and replace them with the 'Language of Value.' If a student can explain a negative coefficient in a churn model as 'Improving our customer service score by one point is linked to a 3% reduction in lost customers,' they have mastered the most difficult part of data science: the human element of the lifecycle.

tasks: Write a one-sentence summary of a regression coefficient for a non-technical manager.
Identify the difference in interpretation between a linear variable and a logged variable in a model.

sessions.title: Diagnostics and Assumptions
sessions.description: This session covers the critical checks required to ensure a regression model is valid, including linearity, homoscedasticity, and independence. You will learn to use residual plots to diagnose model failures and understand the risks of extrapolation. This 'quality control' step is what separates a professional analysis from a potentially misleading one.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by framing the regression model not as a finished product, but as a hypothesis that must be stress-tested. Use the analogy of a bridge: simple and multiple regression gave us the blueprint and the materials, but 'Diagnostics and Assumptions' is the structural integrity test. Explain that the validity of our p-values and coefficients depends entirely on whether the underlying data behaves the way the math expects it to. The core philosophy here is that the 'Errors' (residuals) hold the secrets of where the model is lying. Draw a simple scatter plot and its corresponding residual plot on the whiteboard to show how we shift our gaze from the raw data to the 'leftover' noise.

Introduce the four classical horsemen of regression assumptions—Linearity, Independence, Homoscedasticity, and Normality—using the mnemonic 'LINE.' For Linearity, illustrate on the whiteboard how a curved relationship forced into a straight line creates a 'U-shaped' pattern in the residuals. Explain to students that if they see a pattern in the residuals, it means there is information the model failed to capture. This is a critical moment to teach intuition: a 'good' residual plot should look like a boring, random cloud of dust. If it looks like a shape, the model is missing the story.

Transition to the concept of Homoscedasticity, which often intimidates students due to its name. Simplify it by drawing a 'fan shape' on the board, where the dots spread out as the predicted value increases. Explain that this 'unequal variance' means our model is more certain about some predictions than others, which invalidates our confidence intervals. Use an example like 'predicting household spending based on income': poor households have limited spending options (low variance), while wealthy households might spend very little or very much (high variance). To prevent the common misconception that this 'breaks' the model entirely, explain that it primarily means our 'margin of error' is unreliable, not necessarily that the slope is wrong.

Engage the students in a diagnostic exercise by sketching three different residual plots on the board: one random cloud, one 'U-shape,' and one 'fan-shape.' Ask them to identify which model they would trust for a high-stakes business decision. This practice is designed to move them from 'calculating' to 'inspecting.' It reveals if they can see the qualitative 'health' of a model rather than just looking at the R-squared value, which can often be high even when assumptions are violated.

Conclude by discussing the dangers of Extrapolation and the assumption of 'Independence.' Use the whiteboard to show a regression line ending at the edge of the data range and draw a dotted question mark extending into the void. Explain that the linear relationship we found is only a local truth, not a universal law. Warn them that predicting outside the 'territory' of their data—like using a model of 20-30 year olds to predict the behavior of 80 year olds—is the most common way professional data scientists get into trouble. End the lecture by reinforcing that a model is only as good as the diagnostic tests it survives, and the scientist, can survive.

tasks: Identify heteroscedasticity in a provided residual plot.
List three risks of using a regression model to predict values far outside the range of the training data.

lectures.title: Classification
lectures.description: This lecture introduces supervised learning for categorical outcomes, focusing on how to predict labels and evaluate the performance of discrete classifiers.

sessions.title: Logistic Regression
sessions.description: This session introduces the sigmoid function and the concept of modeling probabilities for binary outcomes. You will learn why linear regression is inappropriate for classification and how logistic regression maps inputs to a 0-to-1 range. This is the entry point into predictive modeling for yes/no questions like churn, fraud, or disease diagnosis.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the intuition established in linear regression. We begin with a binary problem—predicting if a customer will churn or stay—represented as points at exactly 0 and 1 on the y-axis. Draw a standard linear trend line through these points to demonstrate the 'extrapolation failure.' The core idea here is to show that a straight line is structurally incapable of honoring the boundaries of probability; it will eventually predict values like 1.2 or -0.5, which are nonsensical in a yes/no context. This visual tension sets the stage for the necessity of a new mathematical shape.

Introduce the Sigmoid function (or Logistic function) as the 'S-shaped' bridge between the infinite world of linear math and the restricted 0-to-1 world of probability. On the whiteboard, draw the transformation from the linear equation z = mx + b to the sigmoid output. Focus the explanation on the 'squashing' property: how the function takes any real number from negative to positive infinity and maps it into a tight interval. This is the session's most critical conceptual leap: we aren't changing the linear relationship of the features; we are simply wrapping that relationship in a container that makes it interpretable as a likelihood.

Transition to the concept of 'Log-Odds' to explain the 'why' behind the math. Avoid getting bogged down in complex algebra; instead, use the gambling analogy of 'odds' (e.g., 3-to-1) and explain that the logistic regression model is essentially predicting the logarithm of these odds. A common pitfall for students is confusing the raw model output (log-odds) with the final prediction (probability). To address this, conduct a quick 'mental math' check: ask students what a log-odds of 0 represents. Guide them to realize that a log-odds of 0 translates to a probability of 0.5—the point of maximum uncertainty. This practice task helps students internalize that positive log-odds favor 'Yes' and negative log-odds favor 'No.'

Conclude by framing the model's output not as a definitive '1' or '0,' but as a confidence level. Explain that the value 0.85 doesn't just mean the model thinks the answer is 'True'; it means given the evidence (the inputs), there is an 85% probability of the outcome being 'True.' This nuance is vital for data science practitioners because it allows for human-in-the-loop decision-making. Wrap up by hinting at the next session: if we have these continuous probabilities, where do we draw the line to make a final decision? This creates a natural bridge to decision boundaries and thresholds.

tasks: Transform a log-odds value into a probability using the logistic function.
Explain why the output of logistic regression can be interpreted as a confidence level.

sessions.title: Decision Boundaries
sessions.description: This session visualizes how classifiers separate different classes in feature space using decision boundaries. You will learn how changing a probability threshold shifts the boundary and changes which points are classified as 'positive.' This visual understanding helps you grasp how a model makes its 'decisions' and the trade-offs involved in setting thresholds.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by translating the abstract probability output from our previous discussion on Logistic Regression into a physical, geometric reality. On the whiteboard, draw a 2D coordinate system where the x-axis represents one feature—say, 'Study Hours'—and the y-axis represents another—'Sleep Hours.' Plot a scattering of blue circles (students who passed) and red squares (students who failed). The central question to pose is: 'If our model gives us a 0.5 probability of passing, where exactly does that line fall on this map?' This transition is vital because it moves students from thinking about data as rows in a table to thinking about data as positions in space that can be partitioned.

Draw a solid line cutting through the points. This is the 'Decision Boundary.' Explain that this line represents the tipping point where the model's confidence is exactly 50/50. Points on one side are predicted as Class A, and points on the other as Class B. The most critical takeaway here is that while the underlying sigmoid function is a curve in probability space, the boundary it creates in our feature space is a straight line (for basic logistic regression). This is a common point of confusion; students often expect the boundary itself to look like an 'S-curve.' You must clarify that the 'S-curve' describes the probability 'altitude' above this flat map, not the shape of the fence on the ground.

Next, introduce the concept of the 'Threshold.' By default, we use 0.5, but we must challenge the students to think about why we might move it. If we are predicting a rare disease, we might want to be alerted even if the probability is only 0.2. On the whiteboard, show how changing this threshold 'pushes' the decision boundary. A more conservative threshold for predicting 'positive' (requiring 0.8 probability instead of 0.5) will physically shift the line further into the territory of the positive class, effectively shrinking the 'positive prediction zone.' This visualization helps students internalize the trade-off: by being more 'sure' before we label someone as sick, we inevitably leave more sick people on the 'healthy' side of the line.

To solidify this, lead the class through a sketching exercise. Provide a specific scenario, such as a credit card fraud detection system. Ask the students to draw where they would place the boundary if the 'cost' of missing a single fraudulent transaction was much higher than the 'cost' of an annoying but harmless false alarm. Through this, they should realize that the boundary is not just a mathematical derivative, but a policy decision. This prepares them for the next session on error metrics by showing that where we draw the line determines which types of mistakes we are willing to live with.

tasks: Draw a linear decision boundary for a 2D dataset of circles and squares.
Predict how the boundary shifts if the model is adjusted to be more conservative about predicting 'positive' cases.

sessions.title: Confusion Matrices
sessions.description: This session introduces the fundamental tool for evaluating classifiers: the confusion matrix, detailing True Positives, False Positives, True Negatives, and False Negatives. You will learn how to break down model errors to understand exactly where a classifier is failing. This granular view is essential for identifying if a model is biased toward certain types of errors.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by acknowledging that while we now have a model that produces probabilities and decision boundaries, we still face a 'moment of truth'—the point where we compare what we predicted against what actually happened. I will draw a simple 2x2 grid on the board, explaining that this is the 'accounting system' of data science. The goal is to move students away from the lazy comfort of 'accuracy' and toward a forensic understanding of failure. I'll frame the confusion matrix not as a dry table, but as a map of truth versus belief, where we categorize every single prediction into one of four distinct buckets.

I will label the axes clearly: 'Actual' on one side and 'Predicted' on the other. I'll start with the successes—the True Positives (TP) and True Negatives (TN)—noting that these are the instances where our model correctly perceived reality. However, the real pedagogical value lies in the 'off-diagonal' elements. I will deliberately spend more time on the False Positives (FP) and False Negatives (FN). I'll use the analogy of a smoke alarm: a False Positive is the 'nuisance' of the alarm going off for burnt toast (the model cried wolf), whereas a False Negative is the 'catastrophe' of a fire burning while the alarm stays silent. This contrast helps students realize that not all errors are created equal, which is the foundational insight for the rest of the course.

To address common confusion, I will explicitly connect these terms to the statistical language students might encounter elsewhere, specifically 'Type I' and 'Type II' errors. I’ll visualize Type I (False Positive) as a 'False Alarm' and Type II (False Negative) as a 'Missed Detection.' A common pitfall for students is mixing up which axis represents the model's output versus the ground truth; I will mitigate this by teaching them to read the matrix as a sentence: 'The model predicted X, but the reality was Y.' We will then run a quick exercise where I list five hypothetical outcomes (e.g., 'Predicted Cancer/Actual Healthy') and have students call out which quadrant those belong in to build muscle memory.

I will conclude the session by showing that a confusion matrix is the 'source of truth' for every advanced metric we will use later. I’ll emphasize that before we calculate a single percentage or score, we must look at these raw counts. This is where we spot 'bias' in the most literal sense—if a model has 0 False Positives but 100 False Negatives, it isn't 'good' just because it's never wrong when it speaks; it's biased because it's too afraid to speak at all. This transition sets the stage for the next session on evaluating models when simple accuracy fails us.

tasks: Fill out a 2x2 confusion matrix based on a list of actual vs. predicted labels.
Identify which quadrant of the matrix represents a 'Type I error' (False Positive).

sessions.title: Evaluating Classifiers Beyond Accuracy
sessions.description: This session explains why 'Accuracy' is often a misleading metric, especially in imbalanced datasets, and introduces Precision, Recall, and the F1-score. You will learn to choose the right metric based on the cost of different types of errors (e.g., missing a cancer diagnosis vs. a false alarm). This ensures your model evaluation aligns with real-world goals and consequences.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the 'common sense' appeal of accuracy. In a public lecture style, draw a scenario on the whiteboard: a rare disease that affects only 1 out of 100 people. If a student builds a model that simply predicts 'Healthy' for everyone, it achieves 99% accuracy. Ask the class: 'Is this a good model?' This visualization immediately exposes the 'Accuracy Paradox' in imbalanced datasets. The core goal here is to shift the students' mindset from maximizing a single number to understanding the specific costs of being wrong. Explain that accuracy treats all errors as equal, but in the real world, missing a tumor is far worse than a false alarm.

Transition to the concept of Precision. On the whiteboard, draw a circle around all items the model labeled as 'Positive.' Define Precision as the purity of this circle: 'When we scream fire, how often is there actually smoke?' This is critical for scenarios like spam filters where the cost of a false positive (losing a real email) is high. Warn students about the misconception that high precision means the model is 'smart'; it might just be 'timid,' only predicting positive when it is 100% certain, thereby missing many other cases. 

Next, introduce Recall (Sensitivity) by looking at the actual 'Positive' cases in the dataset. Define Recall as the model’s 'reach': 'Out of all the fires that actually happened, how many did we catch?' This is where the life-or-death stakes of data science become visible. Contrast this with Precision using the airport security example. Ask students: 'Would you rather have a scanner with high Precision or high Recall?' This exercise forces them to realize that security prioritizes Recall—it's okay to search a few innocent bags (false positives) if it means catching the one dangerous item. This clarifies that 'best' is a business or ethical decision, not just a mathematical one.

Introduce the F1-Score as the 'diplomat' between Precision and Recall. Explain that you cannot simply average the two because arithmetic means are easily swayed by high outliers. Use the whiteboard to illustrate how the Harmonic Mean (the F1-score) penalizes extreme values. If a model has 100% Precision but 0% Recall, it is useless, and the F1-score will reflect this by dropping to zero. This section is vital for equipping students with a single metric they can use when they need to balance these competing interests in a standard performance report.

Conclude with a hands-on calculation exercise using a mock 2x2 confusion matrix. Have students manually derive Precision, Recall, and F1-score. While they calculate, walk through the room and address the common confusion between the denominator of Precision (Predicted Positives) and Recall (Actual Positives). End by emphasizing that a data scientist's value isn't in generating high scores, but in choosing the metric that best protects the stakeholders from the most 'expensive' type of error.

tasks: Calculate Precision and Recall from a provided confusion matrix.
Decide whether Precision or Recall is more important for a high-stakes scenario like airport security screening.

projects.stage_description: Apply statistical tests to compare store performances and build a classification model to predict whether a customer will churn or become high-value.
projects.deliverable_increment: A 'Model Evaluation Report' including regression coefficients, p-values, and a confusion matrix for the classifier.

exams.goal: Verify the student's ability to apply statistical tests, build regression models, and evaluate binary classifiers using appropriate metrics and diagnostics.

Accurately interpret the coefficients and significance of a multiple regression output.
